html:
An octopus jerks a tentacle away from the hot edge of the aquarium. It has no C-fibers — those thin unmyelinated nerves that in mammals conduct dull, aching pain. Its whole nervous system is built differently: two-thirds of its neurons sit outside the brain, in the tentacles, each arm partly "thinking" for itself. And yet few, watching that recoil, are prepared to say that the octopus feels nothing. If so, then pain cannot be the same thing as the firing of C-fibers. For the octopus has none of them, yet the pain, it seems, is there.

That is the whole argument, in one mollusk. Multiple realizability is the thesis that one and the same mental state can be embodied in physically completely different systems: in a human brain, in an octopus's ganglia, in the silicon innards of a hypothetical Martian, and in the limit — in anything built functionally right. From this follows a conclusion deadly to one influential theory, the type identity theory: a mental state cannot be identified with a particular physical type. The formula "pain = C-fiber firing" is false not because pain is something immaterial but because it ties pain too narrowly to a single physical type. Pain is a role, and a role can have many performers.

The mechanism here is subtle, and it is worth spelling out carefully, so as not to topple into dualism. No one asserts that pain hovers above matter. What is asserted is more modest and more radical: the type of a mental state is determined not by what the system is made of but by what that state does — which inputs cause it, which outputs it produces, with which other states it is connected. Pain is that which is typically caused by injury, produces avoidance, a cry, a memory of danger, and is connected to a desire for it to stop. A causal role. And if the causal role can be played on silicon just as on carbon, then to identify the state with a particular protein or a particular neuron is to confuse the actor with the character. From here a straight road leads to functionalism: the mind as organization, not as substance. And from here, too — the autonomy of psychology: since psychological types "carve" the world differently than neural ones, the science of the mind is not reducible to neuroscience and does not dissolve into it.

How it came about. The thesis was born as a weapon against a specific opponent — the type identity theory, developed in the late 1950s by Ullin Place and John Smart. They asserted: mental states are literally identical to brain states, pain is a particular brain process, just as lightning is an electrical discharge. Hilary Putnam, in the paper "Psychological Predicates" (1967; later reprinted under the title "The Nature of Mental States"), struck with the question of diversity: pain is felt by mammals, reptiles, mollusks, and hypothetically by aliens too. To demand that all of them have one and the same physico-chemical correlate is "certainly an ambitious hypothesis." Hence, Putnam concludes, the identity theory fares worse empirically than functionalism, which makes no such demand. At the time Putnam described the mind in terms of Turing machines: a mental state is a functional state of a probabilistic automaton.

Seven years later Jerry Fodor, in the paper "Special Sciences" (1974), raised the stakes, carrying the thesis from the philosophy of mind into the philosophy of science in general. His example comes from economics. The concept "money" is realized by strings of wampum shells, dollar bills, a signature on a check (today one would add entries on a blockchain); no single physical law covers all exchanges. In just the same way the "special sciences" — psychology, biology, economics — work with types multiply realized in physics, and therefore do not reduce to it while remaining fully materialist. Multiple realizability became not a curiosity about octopuses but a load-bearing beam of the whole non-reductive picture of the world, where the floors of reality are stacked one above another but do not collapse into one.

Criticism / arguments against. The first blow came from neuroscience — and it is serious. William Bechtel and Jennifer Mundale, in the paper "Multiple Realizability Revisited" (1999), noticed that the argument quietly plays fast and loose with levels of description. When we say "pain," we take a coarse-grained, functional concept. When we say "C-fibers," a fine-grained, anatomical one. No wonder the coarse concept maps onto many different fine ones. But one must compare at a single level. And neuroscientists, by the way, identify brain regions across species precisely by function — the hippocampus of a mouse and that of a human share a name not because of identical molecular innards but because of a shared role. If both sides are viewed at the same grain, brains turn out far more alike than the functionalist paints them. Multiple realizability, say Bechtel and Mundale, is rhetorically exaggerated.

The second blow is metaphysical, and it was struck by Jaegwon Kim. In "Multiple Realization and the Metaphysics of Reduction" (1992) and later in the book Mind in a Physical World (1998) he turned the thesis against functionalism itself. If pain-in-a-human and pain-in-an-octopus have nothing physically in common, then what makes both of them pain at all? Only an external similarity of role. But then "pain in general" is not a genuine causal kind but a heterogeneous grab bag, and there can be no scientific laws about it: science will speak separately of pain-in-a-brain and pain-in-silicon. Kim turns the argument inside out: multiple realizability does not save the autonomy of psychology but threatens its unity. And it drags along the famous problem of mental causation: if every mental state is realized by a physical one, and that physical state already has a complete physical cause, then what is left for the mental as such to do? Does the role not turn out to be an epiphenomenon, a powerless passenger on the physical locomotive?

The third, most stubborn question is what "the same" function means on different substrates. Lawrence Shapiro, in "Multiple Realizations" (2000), pointed out that two realizations either differ only in causally irrelevant details (then it is, in essence, the same realization — the color of a corkscrew does not matter for uncorking) or differ in relevant ones (then they are, perhaps, different functions, and one can no longer speak of "the same pain"). Between these blades there is much less room for genuine multiple realization than it seems. And here lies a trap for AI enthusiasts: "the same" is all too easily declared on the basis of coarse behavioral similarity, without asking whether the difference in substrate matters for the very nature of the state.

What to do about it / where it leads. For alignment, multiple realizability is not a museum exhibit but a working premise, often unspoken. The thesis of the substrate independence of the mind, on which transhumanism rests, and talk of mind uploading, and the whole idea that a digital system can possess a full inner world — all are direct children of Putnam and Fodor. If the mind is organization, not substance, then a mind is in principle possible in silicon.

From this follow two conclusions, and both are uncomfortable. The first is about the moral status of AI. If pain really is realizable on a non-biological substrate, then one cannot wave away the question of AI suffering with the phrase "it's just a program, it has no nerves": the absence of nerves is exactly the objection that multiple realizability removes. The threshold beyond which we are obliged to reckon with another's suffering ceases to coincide with the threshold "made of meat."

The second conclusion is cautionary, and it comes from the critics. From the fact that pain in principle can be realized in silicon it does not follow that it is realized in this model. Functional similarity of behavior is too cheap a coin: a language model says "it hurts" splendidly while having, perhaps, nothing behind the words. A separate question is whether reproducing a brain's functional organization would be enough for experience. Ned Block's thought experiment about "the Chinese nation" (the China brain, "Troubles with Functionalism," 1978) — in which a billion Chinese citizens, passing signals by walkie-talkie, realize the functional organization of a brain for an hour — is honed precisely against naive functionalism: a system functionally isomorphic to a human intuitively seems devoid of experiences. The question "is a functional role alone enough for consciousness, or does the substrate matter after all" remains open — and it is in this crack that all the uncertainty of our attitude to the possible suffering of machines lives.

The practical conclusion is modest: multiple realizability forbids us to deny a priori an AI's inner life on the basis of its material substrate, but gives no right to assert it a priori on the basis of behavior. It shifts the burden of proof, it does not abolish it. And it leaves us with a task we have barely approached — to learn to distinguish the realization of pain from its convincing imitation, having access neither to another's C-fibers nor to another's silicon, and not knowing whether there is anyone in there at all for whom it hurts.

  • William Bechtel & Jennifer Mundale. "Multiple Realizability Revisited: Linking Cognitive and Neural States". Philosophy of Science, 66(2), 1999, pp. 175–207.
  • Jaegwon Kim. "Multiple Realization and the Metaphysics of Reduction". Philosophy and Phenomenological Research, 52(1), 1992, pp. 1–26.
  • Lawrence Shapiro. "Multiple Realizations". The Journal of Philosophy, 97(12), 2000, pp. 635–654.
